extracted.intended_audience: painters, art students, and art critics concerned with landscape painting
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging and producing truthful, effective landscape painting—covering tone, color, composition, regional character, scale, and material practice. Draws on examples (primarily Turner) to illustrate virtues and failings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rendering of local / national character
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist must enter thoroughly into the spirit of a country so that local character (vegetation, lines, forms, mood) is convincingly present in a picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of failure include hybrid or 'modern' characters imposed on classical subjects (e.g., Jason with nineteenth‑century legs), or English foliage transposed onto Italian scenes. Successes are simple, small works where local traits are faithfully rendered (vignettes to Rogers's Poems). Anti‑pattern: treating a place as an assemblage of picturesque fragments or using stock 'conventional' motifs (conventional cypresses) instead of observing and drawing the real forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scale and simplicity of subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller, simpler works often convey truth and beauty better than large elaborate compositions; large pictures are prone to being 'overwhelmed with quantity' and deficient in genuine emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text praises small Venetian vignettes and faults many large 'hybrid' pictures (Bay of Baiae, Palestrina) for containing 'ten times as much as is necessary.' Rule: choose subject and scale so that the idea is not sacrificed to accumulations of material. Anti‑pattern: redundancy and excessive detail that obscure the emotional or pictorial focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of composition and emotional direction
rubrics_metrics.description: A good picture should make clear where the eye is to look and what the viewer is to feel; confused or 'nonsense pictures' leave the viewer doubtful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crossing the Brook is praised for tree-drawing but criticized because it 'leaves us doubtful where we are to look and what we are to feel.' Compose so that focal relationships and intended sentiments are unambiguous. Anti‑pattern: mixing incongruent sensations (northern color, southern foliage, England's sensations) without coherent priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and avoidance of mere imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The painter should avoid copying earlier masters conventionally; imitation of Claude or others shows a want of forceful originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When local character is attempted by conventional borrowing, the result appears 'awkward' and cramped. Genuine originality may break conventional rules but must be grounded in truthful perception rather than conventional mimicry. Anti‑pattern: deliberate 'rationalizations of Claude' that produce color and composition faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony between subject and method (don't force methods onto incompatible subjects)
rubrics_metrics.description: One must select methods and effects appropriate to the subject—brilliancy and breadth learned from one landscape-type should not be forced onto scenes where serenity and restraint are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner's error in Italy is described as trying to put 'joyousness and brilliancy of effect upon scenes eminently pensive' and forcing English breadth onto Italy's partitioned spaces. Rule: adapt technique (line, color, handling) to the inherent mood and structure of the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of redundant quantity in elaborate compositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Elaborate compositions often fail from having too many competing elements; quantity should not overwhelm emotional unity and pictorial purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many of Turner's large pictures are 'overwhelmed with quantity' and 'preposterous accumulations' that prevent wholesome feeling. When architecture, foliage, and water compete, each is diminished. Anti‑pattern: sacrificing foliage to architecture or vice versa so that nothing is convincingly any one thing (e.g., water that is 'neither sea, nor river, nor lake').

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of tone: relation of objects in shadow to the principal light
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone (first sense) means the right relation of objects in shadow to the principal light of a picture—accurate relief and relation of objects in darkness and brightness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone requires that the shades of all parts relate properly to the chief light (sky, water, etc.) so the picture reads as under one climate/light. This includes ensuring shadows and illuminated parts are in coherent, perceptible relation. Anti‑pattern: objects looking bright in their own hue but not as raised by illumination, producing lack of 'tone.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone as quality of color influenced by hue of light
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone (second sense) is the quality by which color is felt to owe part of its brightness to the hue of the light upon it—illuminated colors should read as degrees of the same light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colors should be related so illuminated parts and shadows read as different degrees of the same light (warm or cold). The aim is that the whole picture (or tonal areas) be felt to be in one atmosphere. Anti‑pattern: illuminated surfaces appearing as merely their positive hue without evidence of being raised by light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish tone from aerial perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Aerial perspective is the expression of space by means such as edge sharpness and color vividness; it is not identical with tone, which requires the same sum of tonal difference that nature gives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aerial perspective achieves spatial detachment by relative intensity; 'tone' demands that the absolute relations (the sum of differences from foreground to distance) match nature. Beware conflating proportional gradation with the absolute tonal pitches that give nature its full effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of middle tints to the chief light (old masters' strength)
rubrics_metrics.description: Finely toned pictures have middle distances related to the chief light in the same way nature does, albeit often 'an octave or two below' in overall light level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Old masters lowered the whole scale but kept the internal relations; this produces harmonious tone. When attempting tonal lowering, be conscious of material limits (see next item). Use relative pitch between middle tints and light that preserves internal coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical limits of paint vs nature's extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical limitations of pigments and grounds make it impossible to replicate nature's highest lights and deepest voids exactly; this constrains how tone and shadow must be handled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nature's sun and vacuity produce light/dark ranges painters cannot fully match (e.g., our 'deepest shadows' still reflect light). Therefore one cannot give the same absolute pitch of shade as nature throughout without sacrificing intermediate distances. Painterly choices must trade off; attempting to reproduce every natural pitch identically may destroy other essential distances. Guidance: manage the distribution of tonal differences to preserve aerial relations rather than slavishly matching one extreme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rendering of sky, clouds, mountains, stone, and water (specific form and phenomena)
rubrics_metrics.description: Landscape painters must attempt to represent the varied phenomena of the cloudy heavens, mountains, stones, stems of trees, and the surface and movement of water truthfully—these elements have specific, learnable organization and spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asserts Turner uniquely succeeded in drawing many of these elements (sky in all its moods, mountains, tree stems, calm and agitated water, effects of space on distant objects, and natural color). Instruction: study and render the organization/structure of these forms rather than treating them as decorative motifs. Anti‑pattern: generic or schematic handling that misses organization (e.g., conventional cypresses, artificial foliage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foliage and arboreal drawing: specificity and honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Trees and foliage must be drawn with attention to their actual form, branches, and massing—not by conventional or 'affected' shapes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticisms include 'unimaginable finish' of certain French poplars as good examples, and faults where cypresses are 'conventional.' Use direct study; avoid decorative or formulaic leaf/clump shapes. Examples: Ivy Bridge rock foreground praised for delicacy; many later works draw foliage little and poorly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color aims: truthful 'natural color' vs conventional palette
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject conventional palettes that distort natural color (e.g., making whites golden, blues green) in favour of rendering the pure, joyous hues of nature—sky golds, sea azures, conflagration flames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner substituted 'a pure straightforward rendering of fact'—seeking actual roseate hues and intense azure. But such innovation carries peril: new systems of color are difficult and may produce technical faults (overloading, improper representation). Balance ambition with technical means; accept some sacrifice if the pictorial result merits it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of durable materials and care for works
rubrics_metrics.description: Use safe, lasting materials and proper conservation practice; pictures that deteriorate rapidly (cracking, colours losing lustre) fail in material longevity even if visually striking originally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner's practice is criticized for producing pictures that crack or discolor within months or years (Old Temeraire safer; Juliet and her Nurse deteriorated). Recommendation: where desired effects cannot be secured with stable means, either limit production or use safer materials/time-consuming methods to preserve works. Drawings often more secure if properly protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of hand and development of new pictorial canons—accept measured risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovations (new color systems, altered chiaroscuro) may require sacrificing some conventional virtues; a painter's liberty to break rules is defensible if it produces previously unattained pictorial truth or power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text counsels modesty in fault‑finding: some faults are the unavoidable price of new achievement. However, there is unequal success—some experiments fail, and illegitimate licenses or conventionalities are blameworthy. Weigh daring effects against demonstrable avoidable faults; let great ends occasionally justify imperfect means, but not habitual negligence.
